section: England: GCSE maths exam climb, stages 2 and 3 (grades 4 and 5, then Higher)

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 1: Index laws and standard form (grades 4 and 5)
lessons.intention: We are learning to use the index laws and to calculate with numbers in standard form, as the exam asks.
criteria: I can multiply, divide and raise powers using the index laws.
I can write numbers in standard form and back again.
I can multiply and divide numbers in standard form and give the answer in standard form.

steps.start: Ask: is 2³ × 2⁴ equal to 2⁷ or 2¹²? Write out the 2s to settle it.
steps.teach: Show why the laws work by writing powers out in full: multiplying adds the powers, dividing subtracts, a power of a power multiplies. Then standard form: a number from 1 up to (not including) 10, times a power of 10; big numbers have positive powers, small ones negative. For × and ÷ in standard form, deal with the numbers and the powers of 10 separately, then fix the answer if the front number is 10 or more.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (grades 4 and 5) 1: Index laws and standard form" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to work out (6 × 10⁴) × (5 × 10³) and say why 30 × 10⁷ isn't the final answer.

lessons.home: Find the distance to the Moon and the width of a hair online, and write both in standard form.
lessons.vocab: index, power, base, standard form, ordinary number
lessons.understand: Why is 45 × 10³ not in standard form, even though it is the right size?
lessons.lookFor: Says the first number must be at least 1 and less than 10, so it becomes 4.5 × 10⁴.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 2: Percentage change, reverse percentages and interest (grades 4 and 5)
lessons.intention: We are learning to use multipliers for percentage change, to find the original amount, and to work out compound interest and depreciation.
criteria: I can increase or decrease an amount by a percentage with one multiplication.
I can work out a percentage change, dividing by the original amount.
I can find the original amount after a percentage change.
I can work out compound interest and depreciation over several years.

steps.start: A coat is £80 after 20% off. Was it £96 before? Ask them to check by taking 20% off £96.
steps.teach: Turn every percentage change into a multiplier: up 15% is × 1.15, down 15% is × 0.85. Percentage change is change ÷ original × 100. For a reverse percentage, the new price is (100 ± p)% of the old one: divide by the multiplier, never take the percentage of the new price. Compound interest: multiply by the multiplier once a year, so amount × multiplierⁿ; depreciation is the same with a multiplier under 1.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (grades 4 and 5) 2: Percentage change, reverse percentages and interest" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to explain, with numbers, why 20% off then 10% off is not 30% off.

lessons.home: Compare two savings accounts online: which gives more after 3 years?
lessons.vocab: multiplier, percentage change, original amount, compound interest, depreciation
lessons.understand: Why does dividing by 0.8 give the price before a 20% discount?
lessons.lookFor: Says the sale price is 80% of the original, so the original × 0.8 = sale price, and dividing undoes it.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 3: Ratio problems and proportion (grades 4 and 5)
lessons.intention: We are learning to solve harder ratio problems, including three-part ratios and ratio differences, and to use direct and inverse proportion.
criteria: I can share in a ratio with three parts.
I can use a difference between parts to find the total.
I can combine two ratios into one.
I can tell direct from inverse proportion and use each.

steps.start: Two friends share money 3 : 5 and one gets £20 more. How much is there? Ask for a diagram, not a guess.
steps.teach: Draw bar models: each part is a box, so a difference of 2 parts worth £20 makes each box £10. To combine A : B and B : C, make the B numbers the same. Ratio to fraction: parts out of the total. Direct proportion: both go up together, so find one unit first. Inverse proportion: one goes up as the other goes down (more workers, fewer days), so find the total for one worker first.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (grades 4 and 5) 3: Ratio problems and proportion" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to say whether "more workers, fewer days" is direct or inverse, and show how they'd find the time for one worker.

lessons.home: Scale a recipe for 4 people up to 10, and work out how much each ingredient costs per person.
lessons.vocab: ratio, part, bar model, direct proportion, inverse proportion, exchange rate
lessons.understand: How does a bar model help when you know the difference between two shares?
lessons.lookFor: Says the difference is a number of boxes, so dividing finds one box, and then any share or the total.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 4: Expanding and factorising (grades 4 and 5)
lessons.intention: We are learning to expand double brackets, factorise fully, and factorise and solve quadratics.
criteria: I can expand and simplify two brackets, including squaring a bracket.
I can factorise fully by taking out the highest common factor.
I can factorise x² + bx + c and the difference of two squares.
I can solve a quadratic equation by factorising.

steps.start: Ask: is (x + 3)² the same as x² + 9? Try x = 1 in both.
steps.teach: Expand with a grid: four boxes, four terms, then collect the x terms. Squaring a bracket means writing it twice. Factorising fully: the biggest number and letter that go into every term. For x² + bx + c, find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b; check signs carefully. x² − a² is (x + a)(x − a). To solve a quadratic that equals 0, factorise and set each bracket to 0.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (grades 4 and 5) 4: Expanding and factorising" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to factorise x² − 2x − 15 and expand their answer to check it.

lessons.home: Make up three quadratics by multiplying out brackets, then swap with someone to factorise.
lessons.vocab: expand, factorise, quadratic, coefficient, difference of two squares
lessons.understand: Why does setting each bracket to 0 solve (x − 3)(x + 5) = 0?
lessons.lookFor: Says if two numbers multiply to 0, one of them must be 0, so x − 3 = 0 or x + 5 = 0.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 5: Harder equations, simultaneous equations and formulae (grades 4 and 5)
lessons.intention: We are learning to solve equations with brackets and fractions, to form equations, to solve simultaneous equations, and to rearrange formulae.
criteria: I can solve equations with brackets and fractions.
I can form an equation from a problem and solve it.
I can solve two simultaneous equations by elimination.
I can solve inequalities and change the subject of a formula.

steps.start: Two numbers add to 20 and differ by 4. Ask how they'd find them without guessing.
steps.teach: Solve by doing the same to both sides; with a fraction, multiply both sides by the bottom first. To form an equation, name the unknown x and use a fact (angles add to 180°, perimeter). Simultaneous equations: make one letter's numbers match, add or subtract to remove it, solve, then substitute back and check in the other equation. Inequalities work like equations, but write the sign throughout. Changing the subject undoes the formula in reverse order.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (grades 4 and 5) 5: Harder equations, simultaneous equations and formulae" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to solve 3x + 2y = 16 and x − 2y = 0 and check the answer in both equations.

lessons.home: Write an equation for a real situation (two phone deals, a taxi fare) and solve it.
lessons.vocab: solve, simultaneous, eliminate, substitute, inequality, subject
lessons.understand: Why do you substitute back into the other equation at the end?
lessons.lookFor: Says it finds the second letter and checks the pair works in both equations.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 6: Sequences and the nth term (grades 4 and 5)
lessons.intention: We are learning to find and use the nth term of a linear sequence, and to recognise geometric sequences.
criteria: I can find the nth term of a linear sequence.
I can use the nth term to find any term, or which term a number is.
I can decide whether a number is in a sequence, with a reason.
I can continue a geometric sequence.

steps.start: Show 5, 8, 11, 14. Ask for the 100th term without writing them all.
steps.teach: The difference between terms tells you the multiple of n (it goes up in 3s, so 3n). Compare 3n with the sequence to find the adjustment: 3n + 2. To find which term is 302, solve 3n + 2 = 302. A number is in the sequence only if n comes out a whole number. A geometric sequence multiplies by the same number each time.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (grades 4 and 5) 6: Sequences and the nth term" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to decide whether 200 is in 4n + 3, and explain.

lessons.home: Find a pattern in real life (seats in rows, fence panels and posts) and write its nth term.
lessons.vocab: sequence, term, nth term, difference, geometric
lessons.understand: Why does a sequence going up in 3s have 3n in its nth term?
lessons.lookFor: Says 3n goes up in 3s too (3, 6, 9...), so only the start needs adjusting.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 7: Gradients, straight lines and quadratic graphs (grades 4 and 5)
lessons.intention: We are learning to find gradients and equations of straight lines, and to read key points on quadratic graphs.
criteria: I can find the gradient and y-intercept from y = mx + c.
I can find the gradient between two points and the equation of a line through them.
I can recognise parallel lines and find a midpoint.
I can find values and the roots of a quadratic graph.

steps.start: Show y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x − 3 on a grid. Ask what they notice.
steps.teach: In y = mx + c, m is the gradient (up for each 1 across) and c is where the line crosses the y-axis; rearrange first if y has a number in front. Gradient between two points: change in y ÷ change in x. Parallel lines share a gradient. Midpoint: average the x values and the y values. A quadratic graph is a U (or ∩) shape; its roots are where it crosses the x-axis, so solve y = 0.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (grades 4 and 5) 7: Gradients, straight lines and quadratic graphs" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find the equation of the line through (1, 5) and (3, 11).

lessons.home: Plot a phone tariff (fixed charge plus cost per minute) as a straight line and read off its gradient.
lessons.vocab: gradient, intercept, parallel, midpoint, quadratic, root
lessons.understand: What does the gradient of a line tell you?
lessons.lookFor: Says how much y goes up (or down) for each 1 across.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 8: Pythagoras' theorem (grades 4 and 5)
lessons.intention: We are learning to use Pythagoras' theorem to find any side of a right-angled triangle, and in context.
criteria: I can find the longest side (hypotenuse) of a right-angled triangle.
I can find a shorter side.
I can check whether a triangle is right-angled.
I can use Pythagoras for the distance between two points and in real problems.

steps.start: A 5 m ladder, foot 3 m from the wall: how high does it reach? Let them try before teaching.
steps.teach: Label the hypotenuse first: it is opposite the right angle and always the longest. Longest side: square the two shorter sides, add, square root. Shorter side: square the longest, subtract the other square, square root. Check the answer: the hypotenuse must be the longest. For two points, draw the right-angled triangle across and up.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (grades 4 and 5) 8: Pythagoras' theorem" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to explain how they know whether to add or subtract the squares.

lessons.home: Measure a door or a TV screen and check the diagonal with Pythagoras.
lessons.vocab: hypotenuse, right angle, square, square root, Pythagoras' theorem
lessons.understand: How do you know whether to add or subtract the squares?
lessons.lookFor: Says add when finding the longest side (hypotenuse) and subtract when finding a shorter one.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 9: Trigonometry in right-angled triangles (grades 4 and 5)
lessons.intention: We are learning to use sin, cos and tan to find sides and angles in right-angled triangles, and the exact values to know.
criteria: I can label the opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse from an angle.
I can choose sin, cos or tan with SOH CAH TOA.
I can find a missing side and a missing angle.
I know the exact values of sin, cos and tan for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°.

steps.start: Show two right-angled triangles with the same angles but different sizes. Ask what stays the same.
steps.teach: From the marked angle, label the hypotenuse (longest), opposite (across from the angle) and adjacent (next to it). Tick the two sides involved and pick the ratio: SOH CAH TOA. For a side, multiply (or divide, if the unknown is on the bottom). For an angle, use the inverse key (sin⁻¹ and so on). Check the calculator is in degrees. Learn the exact values from the two special triangles.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (grades 4 and 5) 9: Trigonometry in right-angled triangles" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find the angle in a triangle with opposite 5 cm and adjacent 8 cm, saying which ratio and why.

lessons.home: Use an angle and a distance to estimate the height of a tree or building.
lessons.vocab: sine, cosine, tangent, opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse, inverse
lessons.understand: Why do you use the inverse key to find an angle?
lessons.lookFor: Says sin, cos or tan of an angle gives a ratio, so the inverse takes the ratio back to the angle.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 10: Circles, cylinders and prisms (grades 4 and 5)
lessons.intention: We are learning to work out circumference and area of circles, parts of circles, and the volume of prisms and cylinders.
criteria: I can work out the circumference and area of a circle, from the radius or diameter.
I can give answers in terms of π.
I can work out the perimeter and area of a semicircle.
I can work out the volume of a prism and a cylinder.

steps.start: Ask: a pizza is 30 cm across. What is its radius? Its area? Which number goes in πr²?
steps.teach: Circumference is π × diameter; area is π × radius². Check which you are given: halve a diameter before using πr². "In terms of π" means leave π in: 25π. A semicircle's perimeter is half the circumference plus the diameter. A prism's volume is the area of its cross-section × its length; a cylinder is a prism with a circle cross-section.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (grades 4 and 5) 10: Circles, cylinders and prisms" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find the perimeter of a semicircle with diameter 10 cm and explain each part.

lessons.home: Measure a tin and work out how much it holds, then compare with the label.
lessons.vocab: radius, diameter, circumference, π, cross-section, prism, cylinder
lessons.understand: Why does a semicircle's perimeter need the diameter added on?
lessons.lookFor: Says half the circumference is only the curved edge; the straight edge across is the diameter.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 11: Polygons, bearings and similar shapes (grades 4 and 5)
lessons.intention: We are learning to work with angles in polygons, three-figure bearings, scale drawings and similar shapes.
criteria: I can find the sum of interior angles, and each angle of a regular polygon.
I can find the number of sides from an exterior or interior angle.
I can measure and work out bearings, including back bearings.
I can use scales and scale factors for similar shapes.

steps.start: Ask: how many triangles fit inside a hexagon from one corner? What does that tell you?
steps.teach: Interior angles add up to (n − 2) × 180°. Exterior angles of any polygon add up to 360°, so a regular polygon's exterior angle is 360 ÷ n, and its interior is 180° minus that. Bearings: from north, clockwise, three figures. The back bearing is 180° more or less. Similar shapes: find the scale factor from a pair of matching sides, then multiply.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (grades 4 and 5) 11: Polygons, bearings and similar shapes" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find the bearing of A from B when B from A is 060°, with a sketch.

lessons.home: Use a map's scale to work out the real distance of a walk.
lessons.vocab: interior angle, exterior angle, regular polygon, bearing, scale factor, similar
lessons.understand: Why do the exterior angles of any polygon add to 360°?
lessons.lookFor: Says walking round the shape you turn through each exterior angle and end up facing the way you started: one full turn.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 12: Speed, density and pressure (grades 4 and 5)
lessons.intention: We are learning to use compound measures: speed, density and pressure, and to convert their units.
criteria: I can use speed, distance and time, including times in minutes.
I can work out an average speed for a whole journey.
I can use density = mass ÷ volume and pressure = force ÷ area.
I can convert between compound units such as m/s and km/h.

steps.start: Ask: 30 km in 20 minutes. Is that 1.5 km/h? Talk it through.
steps.teach: Write each formula as a triangle or with its units: km/h means km ÷ hours, g/cm³ means grams ÷ cm³, N/m² means newtons ÷ m². Change minutes to hours (÷ 60) before using km/h. Average speed is total distance ÷ total time, never the average of the speeds. To convert m/s to km/h, × 3600 then ÷ 1000.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (grades 4 and 5) 12: Speed, density and pressure" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find the average speed for 1 hour at 40 km/h and 2 hours at 70 km/h, and say why it isn't 55.

lessons.home: Work out the average speed of a journey you made, from the distance and time.
lessons.vocab: speed, density, pressure, compound measure, average speed, units
lessons.understand: What does the unit km/h tell you about how to work out speed?
lessons.lookFor: Says it means kilometres divided by hours, so speed = distance ÷ time.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 13: Tree diagrams, Venn diagrams and relative frequency (grades 4 and 5)
lessons.intention: We are learning to work out combined probabilities with tree diagrams and Venn diagrams, and to use relative frequency.
criteria: I can multiply along branches for AND and add for OR.
I can use 1 − P(none) for "at least one".
I can estimate a probability from results and work out expected numbers.
I can fill in and use a Venn diagram.

steps.start: Ask: what is the chance of two heads in a row? Is it 1/2, 1/3 or 1/4?
steps.teach: Draw a tree: first event, then second event on each branch; probabilities on each set of branches add to 1. Multiply along a path for AND; add the paths that fit for OR. "At least one" is 1 minus "none". Relative frequency = times it happened ÷ trials, and more trials give a better estimate. Expected number = probability × trials. In a Venn diagram, fill the overlap first.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (grades 4 and 5) 13: Tree diagrams, Venn diagrams and relative frequency" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find the probability of at least one six in two rolls, and explain why it's 1 − (5/6)².

lessons.home: Toss a coin 50 times and compare the relative frequency of heads with 0.5.
lessons.vocab: independent, tree diagram, relative frequency, expected, Venn diagram, at least one
lessons.understand: Why is "at least one" easier to work out as 1 − P(none)?
lessons.lookFor: Says there is only one path for "none", but many for "at least one", and together they make 1.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 14: Grouped data and comparing distributions (grades 4 and 5)
lessons.intention: We are learning to estimate the mean from grouped data, find the modal class and the class with the median, and compare two sets of data.
criteria: I can estimate the mean from a grouped frequency table using midpoints.
I can find the modal class and the class containing the median.
I can combine means of two groups.
I can compare two distributions using an average and a measure of spread, in context.

steps.start: Ask: if all we know is that 8 people took 10 to 20 minutes, what time do we use for them?
steps.teach: Grouped data loses the exact values, so use each class's midpoint: sum of midpoint × frequency ÷ total frequency, an estimate. The modal class has the highest frequency. The median is the (n + 1) ÷ 2th value; count through the classes to find it. To combine means, find each group's total first. To compare, give one average and one spread, each with a sentence in context.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (grades 4 and 5) 14: Grouped data and comparing distributions" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to compare two teams' scores with one sentence about the average and one about the spread.

lessons.home: Time a journey on several days and put the times in a grouped table.
lessons.vocab: grouped data, midpoint, estimate, modal class, median, range, consistent
lessons.understand: Why is the mean from a grouped table only an estimate?
lessons.lookFor: Says the exact values are lost, so the midpoints stand in for them.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb, stage 2 start here: check and plan (grades 4 and 5)
lessons.intention: We are finding out which of the grade 4 and 5 topics are already secure and which to learn first, and making a plan for stage 2.
criteria: I can try one exam question on each of the 14 stage 2 topics.
I know which topics I will work on first, and why.
I know how each topic works: lesson, online practice, exam-style sheet, then mini papers.

steps.start: Talk about the goal: a 4 is a standard pass and a 5 a strong pass, and both tiers can give them. Ask which tier the pupil is entered for.
steps.teach: Explain stage 2: 14 topics in order, each with a lesson, online practice and an exam-style sheet; mini papers every few sessions. Stage 3 (Higher, grades 6 to 9) follows for pupils sitting Higher. Do the stage check (online or on paper), with a calculator but no help: it is a map, not a test.
steps.practise: The "GCSE maths climb: stage 2 check (grades 4 and 5)" sheet, or the online stage 2 check.
steps.check: Mark the check together and fill in the "GCSE maths climb: stage 2 tracker (grades 4 and 5)" sheet: the topics that lost marks go first, in climb order.

lessons.home: Look at the tracker together and agree a weekly time for online practice.
lessons.vocab: tier, grade, mark scheme, method mark, secure
lessons.understand: Why work through the topics in the climb's order rather than starting with the hardest?
lessons.lookFor: Says the early topics are used by the later ones, so they make the later topics easier as well as earning marks.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb: what the exam expects (grades 4 and 5)
lessons.intention: We are learning what grades 4 and 5 take, how to choose a tier, and the habits that earn marks on longer questions.
criteria: I know what a grade 4 and a grade 5 mean and roughly what they take.
I can explain the difference between Foundation and Higher.
I use multipliers, formulae and full working on multi-step questions.

steps.start: Show a reverse percentage question answered two ways: one right, one taking the percentage of the new price. Ask which method earns marks.
steps.teach: Go through the "What the exam expects: grades 4 and 5" sheet, then mark the model answers together.
steps.practise: Mark the model answers on the "What the exam expects: grades 4 and 5" sheet together, then the online mixed exam questions with full working on paper.
steps.check: Ask which tier they are sitting and why, and what they will do on a 4-mark question they can't finish.

lessons.home: Do the online mixed exam questions, writing full working on paper.
lessons.vocab: standard pass, strong pass, tier, multiplier, formulae sheet
lessons.understand: Why is Foundation the safer road to a 4, but Higher the only road above a 5?
lessons.lookFor: Says Foundation questions are more familiar so a 4 needs secure basics, while Higher papers are needed for grades 6 to 9.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb: mini papers (grades 4 and 5)
lessons.intention: We are practising exam questions from all the topics together, under exam conditions, and using the results to plan what to revise.
criteria: I can answer mixed exam questions without being told the topic.
I show my working on every question.
I can use my marks to choose which topics to go back to.

steps.start: Recap the exam habits: read twice, underline the command word, show every step, round only at the end.
steps.teach: Set up exam conditions: about 20 minutes, quiet, calculator only for the calculator paper. Remind them to do the questions they can first.
steps.practise: One of the "Mini paper: non-calculator (grades 4 and 5)", "Mini paper: calculator (grades 4 and 5)" or "Mini paper: problem solving (grades 4 and 5)" sheets. Each print is a new paper.
steps.check: Mark it together with the mark scheme, then write the score and the topics to go back to on the tracker.

lessons.home: Redo the questions that lost marks, then the online mixed exam questions.
lessons.vocab: exam conditions, mark scheme, topic, revise
lessons.understand: Your mini paper shows you lost marks on two topics. What do you do next?
lessons.lookFor: Goes back to those topics' lessons or exam sheets before the next mini paper, rather than just doing more papers.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 1: Surds, and negative and fractional indices (Higher)
lessons.intention: We are learning to simplify and calculate with surds, and to work out negative and fractional powers.
criteria: I can simplify a surd using a square factor.
I can add, multiply and expand brackets with surds.
I can rationalise a denominator.
I can work out negative and fractional powers without a calculator.

steps.start: Ask: is √12 the same as 2√3? How could you check without a calculator?
steps.teach: A surd is a root that isn't a whole number; keep it exact. Simplify by finding the biggest square factor: √50 = √25 × √2 = 5√2. Only like surds add. To rationalise k/√n, multiply top and bottom by √n. (a + √b)(a − √b) = a² − b. A negative power means 1 over; a fractional power means a root (the bottom) then a power (the top): 8^(2/3) = (∛8)² = 4.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 1: Surds, and negative and fractional indices" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to work out 27^(−2/3) and explain each step.

lessons.home: Make a set of cards with surds and their simplified forms to match.
lessons.vocab: surd, exact, rationalise, reciprocal, fractional index
lessons.understand: Why is it easier to take the root before the power in 8^(2/3)?
lessons.lookFor: Says the root makes the number smaller first (∛8 = 2), so the power is easy (2² = 4).

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 2: Solving quadratic equations (Higher)
lessons.intention: We are learning to solve quadratics by factorising, by the formula and by completing the square, and to tell how many solutions there are.
criteria: I can factorise and solve quadratics where x² has a number in front.
I can use the quadratic formula and give answers to the accuracy asked.
I can complete the square.
I can use the discriminant to say how many real solutions there are.

steps.start: Ask: can x² + 4x − 7 = 0 be factorised? How else could it be solved?
steps.teach: Try factorising first; for ax² + bx + c, find two numbers that multiply to ac and add to b, and split the middle term. If it won't factorise, use the formula, writing a, b and c (with signs) first and using brackets for negatives. Completing the square: x² + 2px + q = (x + p)² + q − p². The discriminant b² − 4ac tells you: positive, two solutions; zero, one; negative, none.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 2: Solving quadratic equations" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to solve x² + 6x + 2 = 0 by completing the square and by the formula, and compare.

lessons.home: Use a quadratic to find the size of a rectangle with a given area.
lessons.vocab: quadratic, factorise, formula, completing the square, discriminant
lessons.understand: Why does a negative discriminant mean no real solutions?
lessons.lookFor: Says the formula would need the square root of a negative number, which has no real value.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 3: Algebraic fractions and harder simultaneous equations (Higher)
lessons.intention: We are learning to simplify and add algebraic fractions, solve equations with fractions, rearrange harder formulae, and solve a line with a curve.
criteria: I can simplify an algebraic fraction by factorising and cancelling.
I can add algebraic fractions using a common denominator.
I can rearrange a formula where the subject appears twice.
I can solve a linear and a quadratic equation together.

steps.start: Ask: can you cancel the x in (x + 3)/x? Why or why not?
steps.teach: Only whole factors cancel, so factorise top and bottom first. Add fractions as with numbers: common denominator, then add the tops. With fractions in an equation, multiply every term by the common denominator. If the subject appears twice, collect those terms on one side and factorise it out. For a line and a curve, substitute the line into the curve, solve the quadratic, then find y for each x.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 3: Algebraic fractions and harder simultaneous equations" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to make x the subject of y = (x + 2)/(x − 1) and explain the factorising step.

lessons.home: Write your own algebraic fraction that simplifies to x + 1, and swap.
lessons.vocab: algebraic fraction, common denominator, factorise, cancel, subject
lessons.understand: Why can't you cancel the x in (x + 3)/x?
lessons.lookFor: Says x is not a factor of the whole top; only factors that multiply the whole top and bottom cancel.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 4: Functions, iteration and harder sequences (Higher)
lessons.intention: We are learning to use composite and inverse functions, to solve equations by iteration, and to find the nth term of quadratic sequences.
criteria: I can work out composite functions like fg(x), applying the right function first.
I can find an inverse function.
I can use an iteration formula on a calculator.
I can find the nth term of a quadratic sequence.

steps.start: Ask: f doubles a number and g adds 3. Is f then g the same as g then f?
steps.teach: fg(x) means do g first, then f. For an inverse, write y = f(x), rearrange for x, then swap the letter. For iteration, put x₀ in, press = and use ANS for the next one, keeping full accuracy. Quadratic sequences have equal second differences: half of it is the number of n². Subtract that n² part, and the rest is a linear sequence.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 4: Functions, iteration and harder sequences" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find gf(x) and fg(x) for f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = x², and say why they differ.

lessons.home: Find a quadratic sequence in a picture pattern and write its nth term.
lessons.vocab: function, composite, inverse, iteration, second difference
lessons.understand: Why does the order matter in fg(x)?
lessons.lookFor: Says each function changes the input differently, so doing them in another order gives a different result.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 5: Perpendicular lines, circles and turning points (Higher)
lessons.intention: We are learning to work with perpendicular lines, the equation of a circle and its tangent, turning points, graph transformations and areas under graphs.
criteria: I can find a perpendicular gradient and the equation of a perpendicular line.
I can use x² + y² = r² and find a tangent to a circle.
I can find a turning point by completing the square.
I can describe graph transformations and estimate the area under a graph.

steps.start: Show the lines y = 2x and y = −½x crossing. Ask what angle they make.
steps.teach: Perpendicular gradients multiply to −1: the negative reciprocal. A circle with centre the origin is x² + y² = r². A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at that point. Completing the square, y = (x + p)² + q has turning point (−p, q). f(x + a) moves left a, f(x) + a up a, −f(x) reflects in the x-axis, f(−x) in the y-axis. The area under a speed-time graph is the distance.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 5: Perpendicular lines, circles and turning points" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find the tangent to x² + y² = 25 at (3, 4).

lessons.home: Sketch the graph of a journey (speed against time) and find the distance from the area.
lessons.vocab: perpendicular, reciprocal, tangent, turning point, transformation
lessons.understand: Why is a tangent to a circle perpendicular to the radius?
lessons.lookFor: Says the tangent just touches at one point, at right angles to the line from the centre (a circle theorem).

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 6: Direct and inverse proportion, and bounds (Higher)
lessons.intention: We are learning to use proportion with powers and roots, error intervals, upper and lower bounds in calculations, and growth over time.
criteria: I can form and use equations for direct and inverse proportion.
I can write an error interval.
I can choose the right bounds to find the upper or lower bound of a calculation.
I can work out how long growth or decay takes.

steps.start: Ask: a length is 12 cm to the nearest cm. What is the biggest it could be?
steps.teach: Direct proportion: y = kx (or kx², k√x); inverse: y = k/x (or k/x²). Find k from the values given, then use it. A value rounded to the nearest d lies within half of d either side: lower ≤ x < upper. For the upper bound of a sum or product, use both upper bounds; for a division, the upper bound of the top over the lower bound of the bottom. For growth, try powers of the multiplier until it passes the target.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 6: Direct and inverse proportion, and bounds" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find the upper bound of a speed from a distance and a time, explaining which bound of each.

lessons.home: Find out how long savings take to double at a given interest rate.
lessons.vocab: proportional, constant of proportionality, error interval, upper bound, lower bound
lessons.understand: Why does the upper bound of a speed use the lower bound of the time?
lessons.lookFor: Says dividing by a smaller time gives a bigger answer, so the biggest distance over the smallest time is the biggest speed.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 7: Sine rule, cosine rule and 3D trigonometry (Higher)
lessons.intention: We are learning to find sides, angles and areas in any triangle, and lengths in three dimensions.
criteria: I can use the sine rule for a side or an angle.
I can use the cosine rule for a side or an angle.
I can use ½ab sin C for the area.
I can use Pythagoras and trigonometry in 3D.

steps.start: Show a triangle without a right angle. Ask: can SOH CAH TOA find its missing side?
steps.teach: Label sides with small letters opposite their capital angles. Sine rule, a/sin A = b/sin B, needs a side and its opposite angle. Cosine rule, c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C, for two sides and the angle between, or rearranged for an angle when all three sides are known. Area is ½ab sin C. In 3D, find a right-angled triangle inside the shape, often using a diagonal of the base first.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 7: Sine rule, cosine rule and 3D trigonometry" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to choose a rule for a triangle with sides 7 and 9 and the angle between them, and explain why.

lessons.home: Use the cosine rule to find the distance across a field from two measured sides and an angle.
lessons.vocab: sine rule, cosine rule, included angle, opposite, 3D
lessons.understand: How do you decide between the sine rule and the cosine rule?
lessons.lookFor: Says the sine rule needs a matching side and opposite angle; otherwise, with two sides and the angle between or three sides, use the cosine rule.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 8: Circle theorems (Higher)
lessons.intention: We are learning the circle theorems and how to use them, giving reasons, to find angles.
criteria: I can use the angle at the centre, the angle in a semicircle and angles in the same segment.
I can use opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral.
I can use tangent facts: tangent and radius, two tangents from a point.
I can use the alternate segment theorem and give each reason in words.

steps.start: Draw a triangle in a semicircle with the diameter as one side. Ask them to measure the angle opposite the diameter.
steps.teach: Teach one theorem at a time with a sketch: angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference; the angle in a semicircle is 90°; angles in the same segment are equal; opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°; a tangent meets a radius at 90°; two tangents from a point are equal; the alternate segment theorem. In the exam, each angle needs its reason written in words.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 8: Circle theorems" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find an angle and write the reason exactly as the exam would want it.

lessons.home: Make a one-page sheet of the theorems with a sketch of each.
lessons.vocab: circumference, chord, tangent, cyclic quadrilateral, segment, subtended
lessons.understand: Why do circle theorem questions ask for reasons?
lessons.lookFor: Says the marks are for the reasoning: the reason shows which fact makes the angle what it is.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 9: Arcs, sectors, cones and spheres (Higher)
lessons.intention: We are learning to work out arc lengths, sector areas, and the volume and surface area of cones and spheres.
criteria: I can work out the arc length and area of a sector.
I can work out the volume of a sphere, cone and pyramid.
I can work out the surface area of spheres and cones, using Pythagoras for the slant height.
I can give answers exactly, in terms of π.

steps.start: Ask: what fraction of a circle is a 90° sector? A 45° one?
steps.teach: A sector is a fraction of a circle: angle/360 of the circumference for the arc, angle/360 of the area for the sector. Sphere: volume 4/3πr³, surface 4πr². Cone: volume ⅓πr²h, curved surface πrl where l is the slant height (Pythagoras from r and h). A hemisphere's total surface adds the flat circle. Keep π in when asked for an exact answer.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 9: Arcs, sectors, cones and spheres" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find the total surface area of a solid hemisphere and explain each part.

lessons.home: Work out the volume of an ice-cream cone with a hemisphere of ice cream on top.
lessons.vocab: sector, arc, slant height, cone, sphere, hemisphere
lessons.understand: Why does a cone's volume have a third in it?
lessons.lookFor: Says a cone fills a third of the cylinder with the same base and height (the same as a pyramid and its prism).

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 10: Similar shapes: lengths, areas and volumes, and congruence (Higher)
lessons.intention: We are learning how area and volume change in similar shapes, and the conditions for congruent triangles.
criteria: I can use a length scale factor k to find areas (k²) and volumes (k³).
I can work back from an area or volume ratio to a length ratio.
I can go from a volume ratio to an area ratio.
I can say which condition (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS) proves triangles congruent.

steps.start: Show a 1 cm cube and a 2 cm cube. Ask how many small cubes fit in the big one.
steps.teach: If lengths are k times bigger, areas are k² times and volumes k³ times. From an area ratio, square root to get the length ratio; from a volume ratio, cube root. To go from volume to area, cube root then square. Congruent triangles are identical: SSS, SAS, ASA or RHS; three equal angles only shows they are similar.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 10: Similar shapes: lengths, areas and volumes, and congruence" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find the surface area of a larger similar solid from a volume ratio of 8 : 27.

lessons.home: Compare the volumes of two similar tins or bottles and their prices.
lessons.vocab: similar, congruent, scale factor, area factor, volume factor
lessons.understand: Why are volumes multiplied by k³, not k?
lessons.lookFor: Says volume uses three lengths (length × width × height), and each is multiplied by k.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 11: Vectors (Higher)
lessons.intention: We are learning to calculate with column vectors, and to write vectors along paths in a diagram.
criteria: I can add, subtract and multiply column vectors.
I can find the magnitude of a vector.
I can write a vector along a path, such as AB = b − a.
I can use ratio and parallel vectors in vector problems.

steps.start: Ask: to get from A to B, if you know OA and OB, which way do you go?
steps.teach: A column vector says how far across and up. Add and subtract the top and bottom separately; a number in front multiplies both. Magnitude by Pythagoras. In a diagram, travel along known vectors: going backwards along a reverses its sign, so AB = −a + b. A midpoint is half of the way; a point dividing in a ratio is that fraction of the way. Parallel vectors are multiples of each other.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 11: Vectors" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find the vector to the midpoint of AB, and explain each step of the path.

lessons.home: Describe a route on a grid map as a sum of vectors.
lessons.vocab: vector, column vector, magnitude, scalar, parallel, resultant
lessons.understand: Why is AB equal to b − a?
lessons.lookFor: Says from A you go back to O (−a) then out to B (+b).

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 12: Conditional probability and set notation (Higher)
lessons.intention: We are learning to work out probabilities without replacement, conditional probabilities and probabilities in set notation.
criteria: I can use a tree diagram when the second probabilities depend on the first.
I can find a conditional probability from a table or diagram.
I can read and use set notation (∪, ∩, ′).
I can test whether two events are independent.

steps.start: Ask: two socks are taken from a drawer of 3 black and 2 white. Is the second sock's chance the same as the first's?
steps.teach: Without replacement, the second branches change: one fewer of that colour and one fewer altogether. Conditional probability, "given that", means only count the group you are told about. A ∪ B is in A or B or both, A ∩ B is in both, A′ is not in A. Events are independent if P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 12: Conditional probability and set notation" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find the probability two counters taken without replacement are the same colour.

lessons.home: Make a two-way table from your class (for example, pets and siblings) and ask conditional questions about it.
lessons.vocab: conditional, independent, without replacement, union, intersection, complement
lessons.understand: Why do the second branches change without replacement?
lessons.lookFor: Says one item has gone, so there are fewer altogether and fewer of the kind taken.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 13: Histograms, cumulative frequency and box plots (Higher)
lessons.intention: We are learning to draw and read histograms, use quartiles and box plots, and estimate a population by capture-recapture.
criteria: I can work out frequency density and read frequencies from a histogram.
I can find quartiles and the interquartile range.
I can read and compare box plots.
I can estimate a population by capture-recapture.

steps.start: Show a histogram with unequal bars. Ask: which bar has the most people in it?
steps.teach: In a histogram, the area is the frequency: frequency density = frequency ÷ class width. Quartiles split ordered data into quarters; the interquartile range (upper − lower) is the spread of the middle half and ignores extreme values. A box plot shows the lowest, quartiles, median and highest. Compare with the median and the IQR, in context. Capture-recapture: the fraction tagged in the sample matches the fraction tagged in the population.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 13: Histograms, cumulative frequency and box plots" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to compare two box plots with one sentence about the median and one about the IQR.

lessons.home: Collect reaction times from family and draw a box plot.
lessons.vocab: histogram, frequency density, quartile, interquartile range, box plot, capture-recapture
lessons.understand: Why does a histogram use frequency density, not frequency?
lessons.lookFor: Says with unequal class widths a wide bar would look too big; the area shows the frequency fairly.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb 14: Proof, recurring decimals and quadratic inequalities (Higher)
lessons.intention: We are learning to prove results with algebra, disprove them with a counterexample, write recurring decimals as fractions and solve quadratic inequalities.
criteria: I can write an algebraic proof for a fact about numbers.
I can disprove a statement with one counterexample.
I can turn a recurring decimal into a fraction.
I can expand three brackets and solve a quadratic inequality.

steps.start: Ask: 3 + 5 = 8 and 7 + 9 = 16. Does that prove two odd numbers always add to an even number?
steps.teach: Any whole number is n, an even number 2n, an odd number 2n + 1, consecutive numbers n, n + 1. Write the expression, simplify, and finish with a form that shows the result, such as 2(…) for even. One counterexample disproves a claim. For a recurring decimal, multiply by 10 or 100 to line up the repeats, then subtract. For a quadratic inequality, find the critical values and sketch the U-shaped graph.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 14: Proof, recurring decimals and quadratic inequalities" sheet, marked like the exam (method and answer marks), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to prove the sum of two consecutive odd numbers is a multiple of 4.

lessons.home: Find a claim about numbers online and decide whether to prove it or find a counterexample.
lessons.vocab: proof, counterexample, consecutive, recurring decimal, critical value
lessons.understand: Why is one example never a proof, but one counterexample is a disproof?
lessons.lookFor: Says a proof must work for every number, but one case where it fails shows the claim is not always true.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb, stage 3 start here: check and plan (Higher)
lessons.intention: We are finding out which of the grade 6 to 9 topics are already secure and which to learn first, and making a plan for stage 3.
criteria: I can try one exam question on each of the 14 stage 3 topics.
I know which topics I will work on first, and why.
I know how each topic works: lesson, online practice, exam-style sheet, then mini papers.

steps.start: Talk about the goal: grades 6 to 9 on the Higher tier. Higher marks come from long, multi-topic questions and accuracy, not just knowing more topics.
steps.teach: Explain stage 3: 14 topics in order, each with a lesson, online practice and an exam-style sheet; mini papers every few sessions. This is the last stage: it is for pupils sitting the Higher tier. Do the stage check (online or on paper), with a calculator but no help: it is a map, not a test.
steps.practise: The "GCSE maths climb: stage 3 check (Higher)" sheet, or the online stage 3 check.
steps.check: Mark the check together and fill in the "GCSE maths climb: stage 3 tracker (Higher)" sheet: the topics that lost marks go first, in climb order.

lessons.home: Look at the tracker together and agree a weekly time for online practice.
lessons.vocab: tier, grade, mark scheme, method mark, secure
lessons.understand: Why work through the topics in the climb's order rather than starting with the hardest?
lessons.lookFor: Says the early topics are used by the later ones, so they make the later topics easier as well as earning marks.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb: what the exam expects (Higher)
lessons.intention: We are learning what grades 6 to 9 take on the Higher tier, and how top marks are won and lost: accuracy, exact answers, proof and long questions.
criteria: I know roughly what grades 7 and 9 take.
I give exact answers and the accuracy asked for.
I can write a "show that" and a proof properly.
I plan long questions that join topics.

steps.start: Show a quadratic formula answer that loses a sign. Ask the pupil to find the slip and say which marks it still keeps.
steps.teach: Go through the "What the exam expects: Higher, grades 6 to 9" sheet, then mark the model answers together.
steps.practise: Mark the model answers on the "What the exam expects: Higher, grades 6 to 9" sheet together, then the online mixed exam questions with full working on paper.
steps.check: Ask what "in terms of π", "exact" and "show that" each ask for.

lessons.home: Do the online mixed exam questions, writing full working on paper.
lessons.vocab: exact, surd form, show that, proof, accuracy, significant figures
lessons.understand: Why can a correct method still lose marks at Higher?
lessons.lookFor: Says rounding too early, losing a sign or giving a decimal when an exact answer was asked costs the accuracy mark.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb: mini papers (Higher)
lessons.intention: We are practising exam questions from all the topics together, under exam conditions, and using the results to plan what to revise.
criteria: I can answer mixed exam questions without being told the topic.
I show my working on every question.
I can use my marks to choose which topics to go back to.

steps.start: Recap the exam habits: read twice, underline the command word, show every step, round only at the end.
steps.teach: Set up exam conditions: about 20 minutes, quiet, calculator only for the calculator paper. Remind them to do the questions they can first.
steps.practise: One of the "Mini paper: non-calculator (Higher)", "Mini paper: calculator (Higher)" or "Mini paper: problem solving (Higher)" sheets. Each print is a new paper.
steps.check: Mark it together with the mark scheme, then write the score and the topics to go back to on the tracker.

lessons.home: Redo the questions that lost marks, then the online mixed exam questions.
lessons.vocab: exam conditions, mark scheme, topic, revise
lessons.understand: Your mini paper shows you lost marks on two topics. What do you do next?
lessons.lookFor: Goes back to those topics' lessons or exam sheets before the next mini paper, rather than just doing more papers.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: GCSE maths climb: my next step (working on your own, grade 1 to 9)
lessons.intention: We are learning to follow the climb on our own: take the check, practise the next topic, mark our work like an examiner and know when to move on.
criteria: I can open the climb page and follow My next step.
I read the mark scheme after every question, even when I was right.
I can mark my own working with method and answer marks.
I know when a topic is secure and when to move to the next stage.

steps.start: Ask: when you study on your own, how do you decide what to do next? Talk about why guessing wastes time.
steps.teach: Open popspell.com/climb.html together. Show My next step: it starts with the stage check, then picks the first topic that needs work, in the climb's order, and suggests a mini paper when a stage is nearly done. Show where the mark scheme appears after each answer and how a topic becomes secure (three-quarters of the marks on a practice set). Explain that progress stays on this device only. For working on paper or offline, show popspell.com/pack.html: it makes a whole stage as one PDF with the answers at the back.
steps.practise: The "GCSE maths climb: my route from grade 1 to 9" sheet: fill in the exam date and target together, then do one practice set on the climb page.
steps.check: Ask them to show you their next step on the climb page and explain why that topic comes next.

lessons.home: Two or three sessions a week on the climb page, about 45 minutes each, with a notebook for working. No internet at home, or rather work on paper: download the pack for their stage from popspell.com/pack.html (every sheet, a plan to tick off, and the answers at the back).
lessons.vocab: self-guided, mark scheme, secure, stage, next step
lessons.understand: Why read the mark scheme even when you got the answer right?
lessons.lookFor: Says it shows which lines of working earn marks, so you can write them in the exam even when the last step goes wrong.
